draft.title: Chemical changes
card: In a chemical change, the atoms in the starting substances rearrange to make new substances. The atoms are not created or destroyed. They join up in a different way.
The new substances have different properties from the starting ones. Iron and oxygen make rust, which is crumbly and reddish-brown, not hard and grey.
A chemical change is usually hard to reverse. You cannot easily turn ash and smoke back into wood.
Compare a physical change, where no new substance forms. Ice melting is still water, so it is not a chemical change.
draft.remember: Chemical change: atoms rearrange into new substances, and it is usually hard to undo.

a.q: Which statement best describes what happens to atoms in a chemical change?
opts: They rearrange to form new substances
They are destroyed and replaced by new atoms
They stay joined in the same way as before
They turn into a different state of matter
a.why: In a chemical change the same atoms join up in new ways, so new substances form. The atoms are not destroyed. Staying joined the same way would mean no new substance forms.
a.clue: Think about what happens to the atoms, not whether they vanish.

b.q: Lena fries an egg. The clear, runny white turns into a firm white solid that cannot be turned back. Why is this a chemical change?
opts: New substances formed and it cannot easily be reversed
The egg white changed from a liquid to a solid
The egg white changed its shape in the pan
The egg white is now hotter than it was before
b.why: The egg proteins rearranged into new substances with new properties, and cooling the egg does not undo it. A change of state alone can be a physical change, as when water freezes, so it does not prove a chemical change.
b.clue: Ask whether a new substance has formed.

a.best: They rearrange to form new substances

b.best: New substances formed and it cannot easily be reversed

proposal.title: Chemical changes
card: In a chemical change, the atoms in the starting substances rearrange to make new substances. The atoms are not created or destroyed. They join up in a different way.
The new substances have different properties from the starting ones. Iron and oxygen make rust, which is crumbly and reddish-brown, not hard and grey.
A chemical change is usually hard to reverse. You cannot easily turn ash and smoke back into wood.
The test is whether a new substance forms. A change in shape or state, or mixing two things, does not prove a chemical change. Melting is a physical change instead.
proposal.remember: Chemical change: atoms rearrange into new substances, and it is usually hard to undo.

a.q: Which statement best describes what happens to atoms in a chemical change?
opts: They rearrange to form new substances
They are destroyed and replaced by new atoms
They stay joined in the same way as before
They turn into a different state of matter
a.why: In a chemical change the same atoms join up in new ways, so new substances form. The atoms are not destroyed. Staying joined the same way would mean no new substance forms.
a.clue: Think about what happens to the atoms, not whether they vanish.

b.q: Lena fries an egg. The clear, runny egg white turns into a firm white solid. Why is this a chemical change?
opts: A new substance with different properties formed
The egg white changed from a liquid to a solid
The egg white spread out and changed its shape
The egg white mixed with the oil in the pan
b.why: The atoms in the egg white rearranged into a new substance with new properties, and cooling the egg does not undo it. Going from liquid to solid is tempting, but a change of state alone does not prove a chemical change, as water freezing shows.
b.clue: Ask whether a new substance has formed.
